We accept that the Appellant has raised serious and thoughtfully presented concerns. However, when we step back and assess the material holistically, as section 14(1) requires, the cumulative picture remains decisive.
We find on the balance of probabilities (and based on the evidence before us):

The Appellant submitted 32 FOIA requests to FOS between February and December 2022, all relating to FOS’s handling of his complaint against AXA. They were often multipart and broad, seeking internal guidance, Discovery content, training materials, call handling/recording procedures, IT storage data, a broadcast copy of
Dispatches
, and information about decision publication. These were accompanied by a significant volume of follow-up correspondence, clarifications and related emails during 2022 and early 2023.
These were part of a series of requests made between 27 January 2020 and 1 June 2023. In total there 110 requests during this period.

Contemporaneous records show that, during this period, FOS received large quantities of communications from the Appellant, including FOIA requests, internal review requests, subject access requests, and other emails. The evidence indicates that messages were sometimes sent in rapid succession and, on occasions, copied to broad distribution lists. The Appellant did not accept all of FOS’s figures, but the overall pattern of sustained and high volume contact was established on the materials before the Tribunal.

We find that responding to these requests would have required coordinated work across several FOS departments and placed significant operational pressure on the organisation, including a temporary backlog in its email systems.

We conclude that the Appellant’s sincere dissatisfaction with FOS’s handling of his complaint does not alter the fact that FOIA was being used inappropriately to perpetuate a dispute wholly outside FOIA’s statutory function.

The Appellant’s communication style and frequency were influenced by his personal circumstances, including diagnosed Autism/Asperger’s and associated anxiety disorders. He was motivated by genuine concerns and acted in good faith. However, some requests/emails used accusatory terms about staff conduct and were sent in large batches to extensive distribution lists; the tone and pattern showed that the objective effect of the correspondence, regardless of intention, was a significant demand on FOS’s resources.

There is no evidence that the Appellant intended to cause disruption or distress and that he believed his requests were necessary. Nonetheless, on the basis of contemporaneous documentation and the parties’ evidence, the combined volume, breadth and tempo of the requests and related emails placed a substantial and sustained burden on FOS during the period covered by the DN.

Many requests were closely connected to the Appellant’s continuing wish to revisit or understand the handling of his underlying complaint, which FOS had already indicated was closed, and that while some topics had potential wider interest, a significant proportion related specifically to his own case.
The Tribunal therefore finds that the burden imposed was exceptional, and that this factor weighs strongly in favour of section 14(1).

We add that, even if all the Appellant’s concerns about the handling of his AXA complaint, the internal processes followed by FOS, and the accuracy of material disclosed to him were assumed to be entirely correct, this would not alter the outcome under section 14 FOIA. The statutory question before the Tribunal is confined to whether the character, scale and cumulative effect of the Appellant’s information requests and associated correspondence, during the period addressed in the DN, amounted to a disproportionate and unreasonable use of FOIA. The test under section 14(1) is concerned with the
impact

of the requests on the public authority’s resources, not the underlying merits of any grievances or allegations. Even taking the Appellant’s account at its highest and fully recognising why he felt compelled to seek clarity and transparency, the evidence demonstrates that the volume, breadth and frequency of the requests imposed a very substantial burden on FOS. That burden would not materially alter our assessment under s.14(1). Accordingly, those wider matters, even if assumed in his favour, do not displace the Tribunal’s conclusion that FOS was entitled to rely on section 14(1).

When all factors are taken together: volume, persistence, complexity, purpose, value and effect, the cumulative picture supports the Commissioner’s conclusion that section 14(1) was properly engaged. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed and the Decision Notice is upheld.

As one final note, we wish to acknowledge the considerable care, effort and detail the Appellant has brought to his submissions. This decision is not a judgment on the merit or sincerity of his concerns about FOS. It reflects only FOIA’s statutory limits and the need for public authorities to manage substantial resource burdens reasonably.
